title: Family & people
goal: Talk about your family, say whose something is, and use the singular and plural of common nouns.
intro:
Family is the centre of Pashtun life, and the vocabulary is precise: there are different words for your father's brother (تره) and your mother's brother (ماما), and even a special word for a cousin on your father's side (تربور).

In this unit you'll learn family words, two ways of saying 'my' (the full word زما and the little clitic مې), and how Pashto nouns show gender and plural. You'll also meet the **oblique case** — the form a noun takes after د 'of'.

grammar.title: Saying 'my, your, his': full possessives and clitics
grammar.body:
Pashto has two ways to show possession.

**1. Full possessive words**, placed before the noun:
زما zmā my · ستا stā your (inf.) · د هغه də haġə́ his · د هغې də haġé her · زموږ zmuẓ our · ستاسو stāso your (pol./pl.) · د هغوی də haġwí their

**2. Short unstressed clitics**, which are extremely common in speech:
مې me (my) · دې de (your, inf.) · يې ye (his/her/their) · مو mo (our / your pl.)

The clitics don't stand before the noun: they slip into the **second position** of the sentence, right after the first word or phrase. So 'my father is a doctor' is پلار مې ډاکټر دی (lit. father-my doctor is). Clitics are used for other jobs too, as you'll see later — but 'my/your/his' is the place to start.

examples.native: مور يې په کور کې ده.
examples.roman: mor ye pə kor ke da.

grammar.title: Gender and plural of nouns
grammar.body:
Every Pashto noun is **masculine** or **feminine**. The ending usually tells you:
• Masculine: ends in a consonant (کور kor, هلک halə́k) or in **-ay ی** (سړی saṛáy).
• Feminine: ends in **-a ه** (ښځه ṣədzá, مڼه maṇá) or **-əy ۍ** (نجلۍ njlə́y).
Natural gender wins: پلار 'father' and مور 'mother' are masculine and feminine whatever their endings.

Common plural patterns:
• Masculine people/animals add **-ān**: هلک → هلکان, ماشوم → ماشومان
• Masculine things add **-una**: کور → کورونه korúna, نوم → نومونه
• Masculine -ay becomes **-i**: سړی → سړي, ملګری → ملګري
• Feminine -a becomes **-e**: ښځه → ښځې, خبره → خبرې
• Feminine -əy stays the same: کړکۍ → کړکۍ
Family words are often irregular (وروڼه، خويندې، زامن، لوڼې، نجونې) — learn them with the noun.

grammar.title: The oblique case after د 'of'
grammar.body:
Pashto nouns change form depending on their role. The basic form (the **direct** case) is used for subjects. After **د** 'of' and after most prepositions, nouns go into the **oblique** case.

In the singular, only some nouns change:
• masculine -ay → -i: سړی → د سړي də saṛí 'the man's'
• feminine -a → -e: ښځه → د ښځې də ṣədzé 'the woman's'
• most masculine nouns ending in a consonant don't change: د احمد، د پلار
In the **plural**, every noun's oblique ends in **-o**: د هلکانو də halakā́no 'of the boys', د ښځو də ṣədzó 'of the women'.

Note the order: owner first, thing owned second, just like English 'Ahmad's house': د احمد کور.

dialogue.title: Family photos
dialogue.setting: Zarmina shows her university friend Lina photos on her phone.

lines.speaker: Zarmina
lines.native: دا زما کورنۍ ده. دا زما پلار دی، او دا مې مور ده.
lines.roman: dā zmā kornə́y da. dā zmā plār day, aw dā me mor da.
lines.en: This is my family. This is my father, and this is my mother.

lines.speaker: Zarmina
lines.native: دا زما کشر ورور دی. نوم يې ميرويس دی.
lines.roman: dā zmā kə́shər wror day. num ye mirwáys day.
lines.en: This is my younger brother. His name is Mirwais.

lines.speaker: Lina
lines.native: ته څو وروڼه او خويندې لرې؟
lines.roman: tə tso wróṇa aw xwínde lare?
lines.en: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

lines.speaker: Zarmina
lines.native: دوه وروڼه او درې خويندې. زما مشره خور واده شوې ده.
lines.roman: dwa wróṇa aw dre xwínde. zmā mə́shra xor wādə́ shə́we da.
lines.en: Two brothers and three sisters. My older sister is married.

lines.speaker: Zarmina
lines.native: زموږ تربور دی. دوی يو ماشوم هم لري.
lines.roman: zmuẓ tarbúr day. duy yaw māshúm ham lári.
lines.en: He's our cousin. They also have a baby.

lines.speaker: Lina
lines.native: ډېره ښکلې کورنۍ ده. ماشومان دې روغ وي!
lines.roman: ḍéra ṣkə́le kornə́y da. māshumā́n de roġ wi!
lines.en: It's a very beautiful family. Bless your little ones!

culture: Pashtun families are large and close, and several generations often live in one house or compound. Respect for elders (مشران) is central: the eldest man usually speaks for the family, and you stand when an elder enters. Cousins on the father's side (تربور) share land and family honour — and the word تربورولي (tarburwalí) has come to mean the rivalry that can exist between them, a theme of countless proverbs and stories. Don't ask a man directly about his wife or daughters by name; asking about 'the family' or 'the children' (کورنۍ، ماشومان) is polite and normal.
